claims.text: The mixed noble-metal precursor complexes inherently have diverse reduction and decomposition characteristics.
Uniformly tailoring the ligand complexes on each precursor can align ligand decomposition and metal-reduction onset.
Complete ligand removal can be achieved or verified after reduction.
A moderate synthesis temperature range of approximately 150–250 °C is applicable to the proposed process.
Aligned ligand-decomposition profiles produce uniform reduction kinetics and synchronized nucleation.
Synchronized nucleation minimizes local concentration fluctuations.
Synchronized reduction causes all noble-metal species to begin forming nuclei at approximately the same time.
Synchronized nucleation limits atomic diffusion or the time window available for stochastic diffusion.
Limiting the diffusion window suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation.
Limiting the diffusion window suppresses non-uniform nanoparticle morphology.
The tailored-ligand intervention will promote homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The resulting single-phase nanoparticles will have an FCC crystal structure.
The tailored-ligand nanoparticles will have a more uniform elemental distribution and better-controlled morphology than the conventional-precursor baseline.
The tailored-ligand route will reduce the effective decomposition temperature relative to conventional precursors.
Conventional, non-uniform ligand environments cause asynchronous reduction kinetics.
Asynchronous reduction kinetics in the conventional baseline lead to phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology.
The hypothesis applies to noble-metal systems containing more than five elements under moderate, controlled heating in an inert atmosphere.
Failure to align ligand-decomposition temperatures, or persistence of ligand residues, may prevent the proposed approach from succeeding.
Small mismatches in ligand-decomposition temperatures may cause partial elemental segregation.
